2027-03-09.title: Tuesday of the Fourth Week of Lent
readings: I saw water flowing from the temple, and all who were touched by it were saved
The Lord of hosts is with us; our stronghold is the God of Jacob
At once the man was made well
2027-03-09.alt: Lenten weekday. The Gloria and the Alleluia are omitted throughout Lent. Liturgical colour: violet. Commemoration of St Frances of Rome, religious (her collect may be used).
2027-03-09.verse: When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be made well?”
theo: Today's readings are full of water. In Ezekiel's vision an angel leads the prophet to the door of the Temple, and from under the threshold a stream is flowing east. The angel measures a thousand cubits and the water is ankle-deep; another thousand and it is knee-deep; then up to the waist; then “a river that could not be crossed.” This river flows down into the Dead Sea, the lowest and saltiest water on earth, where nothing lives, and makes it fresh: “everything will live where the river goes.” On its banks grow trees whose fruit never fails and whose “leaves are for healing,” “because the water for them flows from the sanctuary.” Lent is leading the elect toward the waters of Baptism, and leading all of us to renew our own. The Psalm sings of the same river: “There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God,” for “the LORD of hosts is with us.”

The Gospel takes us to a pool in Jerusalem, Beth-zatha, with five porticoes full of the blind, the lame and the paralysed. Archaeologists have uncovered its great basins near the Sheep Gate. One man has been ill for thirty-eight years, almost a lifetime. Jesus sees him, knows how long he has lain there, and asks a surprising question: “Do you want to be made well?” The man's answer is the saddest sentence in the passage: “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool.” Then Jesus does what the water never did for him: “Stand up, take your mat and walk.” At once he is healed. Because it is the sabbath, the authorities object; John, writing after the break between Church and synagogue, often uses “the Jews” for these Temple leaders who opposed Jesus, not for the Jewish people as a whole, whom the Church honours as the people of the covenant. Later Jesus finds the man in the Temple: “See, you have been made well! Do not sin any more.” The healing of the body points to the deeper healing of the soul. The true river from the Temple is Christ himself, and his water reaches us in Baptism and in Confession. Today we also remember St Frances of Rome (1384–1440), a noblewoman married at thirteen, mother of three, who nursed the sick through plague and war, opened her house to the poor, and founded a community of Oblates. She used to say (in substance) that a wife and mother must sometimes leave God at the altar to find him in her housework. For many, she was the someone who carried them to the water.
outline: Ask: is there anyone in your life who could say, “I have no one”?

live: Bless yourself slowly with holy water today, remembering the river that first touched you.
Find one person who has no one to help them, and help them this week.
2027-03-09.prayer: Lord God, from your sanctuary flows a river that brings life wherever it goes. Let the waters of Baptism heal what is sick in us, and give us the courage to answer Jesus when he asks if we want to be made well. Through the prayers of St Frances of Rome, make our homes places of prayer and service. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: From the pierced side of Christ on the cross flowed blood and water, the river of the sacraments. At the altar we drink from that river, and it makes us live.

quick: Ezekiel sees a river flowing from the Temple that brings life wherever it goes.
Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years and had no one to help him.
St Frances of Rome served God in her family and in the poor.
2027-03-09.action: Help one person today who has no one to help them.
2027-03-09.question: Do I really want to be made well, or have I grown used to my mat?

family.explain: A man had been sick for thirty-eight years. He had no friend to help him into the healing pool. Jesus asked him: do you want to get well? Then he said: stand up and walk! And the man walked. Jesus wants to heal us too, and he wants us to help people who are alone.
family.intention: We pray for people who are sick for a long time, and for those who are lonely.
family.ask: Ask: “Who in our family, school or street has no one? What can we do for them?”

illus: In a coastal parish near Kollam, an elderly fisherman who could no longer walk sat for years at his window watching people go to Sunday Mass. One Lent a group of teenagers decided to take turns pushing his wheelchair to church. On the first Sunday he wept at the door. He said: for eleven years I had no one; today I have six grandsons I never knew I had.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, river of life, you see us lying by the water and ask if we want to be made well. Heal us and make us helpers of others. Amen.
share: Everything will live where the river goes (Ezekiel 47:9). Where does my life need the river of God?
Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool (John 5:7). Who around me has no one?
Do not sin any more (John 5:14). What healing of the soul do I need this Lent?
pm.resp: The Lord of hosts is with us; our stronghold is the God of Jacob.
interc: For the elect preparing for Baptism at Easter, that the living water may make them new.
For the chronically ill and those who care for them over many years.
For the lonely and forgotten, that they may find someone who helps.
For wives and mothers, through the prayers of St Frances of Rome.
For our group, that we may be someone's someone this week.
pm.close: Father, the river from your sanctuary heals and gives life. Let it flow through us to those who have no one. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Ezekiel sees water flowing from under the door of the Temple. It grows from ankle-deep to knee-deep to a river that could not be crossed. It flows into the Dead Sea and makes it fresh: wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live (Ezekiel 47:9). That river is a picture of grace, and we first stepped into it at our Baptism.

In the Gospel there is a pool full of sick people, and one man who has been ill for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks him: do you want to be made well? (John 5:6). It is not a foolish question. Sometimes we grow used to our illness, our sin, our sadness, and we stop hoping.

The man answers: sir, I have no one to put me into the pool. Thirty-eight years, and no one. Then Jesus says: stand up, take your mat and walk. And he walks. Later Jesus tells him: do not sin any more. Jesus heals the body, but he wants to heal the soul even more. That is why we go to Confession in Lent.

Today we remember St Frances of Rome, a wife and mother who nursed the sick through plague and war and opened her home to the poor. She found God at the altar and in the kitchen. Let us ask Jesus to heal us, and let us become, like her, someone for those who have no one. Amen.
kids: Children, a man was sick for thirty-eight years, and he had no friend to help him. Jesus came and said: stand up and walk! And he walked. Jesus is a friend to people who are alone. Can you be a friend to someone who is alone at school?

intro: Theme: “Do you want to be made well?”
The river from the Temple, the man who had no one, and a saint who carried others to the water.

q: Wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live, and there will be very many fish, once these waters reach there. It will become fresh; and everything will live where the river goes.

points.apply: Name the sin you have grown used to, and bring it to Confession this Lent.

sub: Frances of Rome: altar and kitchen.
q: Is it not to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover them, and not to hide yourself from your own kin?
Bear one another's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.

concl: The river of grace flows from Christ, the true Temple, and makes the dead live.
Jesus asks if we want healing, and sends us to those who have no one.
